newsitem.title: UK: Softs outlook - LIFFE contracts seen trending mixed.
newsitem.headline: Softs outlook - LIFFE contracts seen trending mixed.

text.p: LIFFE's robusta coffee may scoop some gains this week but the outlook for cocoa and sugar futures stays bleak, analysts said.
Coffee regained strength late last week on the back of steep New York gains and fund buying, pushing London's benchmark January to $1,476 a tonne, the highest level since mid-October.
It pulled back to end Friday $5 up at $1,460. The contract had been trapped in $1,365-$1,410 band for the past few weeks.
No new fundamental factors were cited, just the continuing appreciation that the physical market is tight and supplies from Central America are not due in large amounts until December.
Coffee's technical picture may also alter, traders said.
"From the technical perspective...there might be a trend change in coffee," said one.
"We had a very long consecutive downtrend and I just wonder if we are going to have a minor return to an uptrend," he said.
U.S. certified coffee stocks have never been so low, buoying the nearby Dec/March spread which stood at a hefty 13 U.S. cents a lb by late Friday.
"Whether December is squeezed ahead of the first notice day on November 19 is the question on everyone's lips," broker GNI said.
In physical news, the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) technical committee met over the weekend to review the market at a session in Costa Rica.
Many roasters, traders and producers are also away this week for Costa Rica's annual international coffee week, Sintercafe, which follows the ACPC meeting.
In cocoa, traders said the market seemed to have attempted a minor consolidation last week.
But industry buying remained low with grinders being hampered by rising sterling against major currencies.
Besides currency, the market is also keeping an eye on cocoa arrivals from Ghana and Ivory Coast, two top growers.
"If no surprises take place, I suspect the market will maintain a generalised range, possibly work a little bit lower if origins are more aggressive," he said.
Others said a feeling of inertia had surrounded the futures again after a brief of correction from the lows seen last week.
"We will have to either move down to a new low area or move above 950 (basis March) to see what sort of selling there is," said one.
Benchmark March ended Friday two stg lower at 934 stg a tonne. It traded at 945 stg a week ago.
Analysts also kept a bearish view on London's white sugar futures, which traded at around $306.90 a tonne late on Friday for December, down from $308.20 a week ago.
Sugar's outlook hinged on fresh physical demand.

"Perhaps for the time being the market may be near the lows but I would imagine over the course of this week if there is no further offtake the market would start its way back down again," said one. -- London newsroom +44 171 542 4985
